data.title: Rubio floats CIA 'partnership' to Cubans tired of 'failed promises, corruption'
data.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered Cubans a discreet CIA partnership opportunity in a Friday social media post, saying “now is the time” for those looking to “create positive change” in the Caribbean country.

“The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said in a post to the social platform X.

The U.S. government has offered CIA partnerships to residents of adversarial countries in the past, namely in Russia — where the agency launched a Telegram campaign in 2023 to encourage intelligence sharing.

Rubio’s post came after Trump again suggested the U.S. could take military action in Cuba at a rally in Fort Myers, Fla.

“We’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran,” Trump said. “Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re gonna send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

The president’s rhetoric on Cuba has escalated throughout the year. In March, Trump said “Cuba is next” after the Iran war and that he would have the “honor” of taking over the country.

The island nation has struggled with blackouts and supply shortages as the Trump administration has increased pressure on its communist regime through sanctions and an oil blockade. Rubio said last month that Cuba was a “failed state.”

“Well, the truth is Cuba has already fallen,” Rubio told Fox New commentator Sean Hannity.

Still, it is unclear whether Trump plans to follow up on his threats of military action against Cuba. Throughout the Iran war, the president has threatened to destroy the Islamic Republic’s energy infrastructure and once warned “a whole civilization” would die unless “something revolutionarily wonderful” happened before a time limit he set — only for the U.S. to back off before the deadline.

data.title: Peltola calls Alaska lawsuit a 'desperate attempt' for GOP to 'cling to power'
data.description:
Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola (D) responded to the Justice Department’s (DOJ) lawsuit seeking to block her state from certifying its election results should her Republican challenger lose, saying Friday the move was “frivolous.”

“This is clearly corruption. This is clearly a very desperate attempt to cling to power, using his allies in Washington, D.C. to rig the system even further,” Peltola, a former member of Congress, told MS NOW’s Nicolle Wallace.

The DOJ filed a lawsuit Friday seeking to block the certification of Alaska’s Senate race if anyone other than Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan wins. The department claimed that, since another candidate shares the same name as the GOP senator, the election results may be inaccurate.

The ballot includes Sen. Sullivan’s Republican affiliation and incumbent status to differentiate him from the other candidate in question, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

“Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election,” the filing reads.

Peltola said Friday she believes Alaska voters can tell the difference between the two candidates on the ballot and any argument otherwise is “not playing well with Alaskans.”

“It’s sending a message that Dan Sullivan does not believe that Alaskans are sophisticated enough to know exactly who they’re voting for and what the implications of their vote is,” Peltola said.

The Center for Election Innovation and Research (CEIR), a nonprofit aiming to build confidence in U.S. elections, called the DOJ’s lawsuit “an unprecedented intervention.”

“This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election,” CEIR Executive Director David Becker said in a statement. “The DOJ attempting to intervene at this late stage is entirely against department policy.”

Democrats widely condemned the move, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who called the lawsuit an “outrage” in a post to the social platform X Friday evening.

“This is an outrage. It shows they know they’re going to lose. We will fight tooth and nail. And we will win,” Schumer wrote.

The former Alaska lawmaker said she was not sure whether Sullivan supported the DOJ’s legal strategy. In an earlier statement sent to The Hill, the incumbent senator’s campaign spokesperson Nate Adams said his team would “let the DOJ complaint run its course.”

The president has repeatedly amplified unsubstantiated mass voter fraud claims, namely toward blue states. A new poll from the New York Times/Siena University found half of Americans believe Republicans may attempt to overturn the midterm results through illegal means.

Peltola there has never been a reason to doubt the security of Alaska’s election system.

“We’ve been running great elections for decades.  There have never really been any abnormalities or irregularities to speak of,” Peltola said. “I have total confidence in Alaskans’ ability to know who they’re voting for.”

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Peltola a 61 percent chance of winning the Alaska Senate race.

data.title: Kennedy rolls out US-caught seafood labeling, Seafood.gov
data.description:
The Trump administration unveiled new initiatives for U.S. fishermen Friday, including a new government website known as Seafood.gov.

At a rally in Fort Myers, Fla., Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the creation of a voluntary label made for U.S.-caught fish, which the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began offering Friday, the White House said.

Kennedy said at the rally that fish caught in the U.S. is of higher quality than European-caught and imported seafood.

“No European country will take them, so they ship them all over here,” Kennedy said, referring to shrimp. “President Trump is rebuilding the infrastructure, he’s reopening the markets for our commercial fishermen.”

Data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) shows that in 2023, an estimated 80 percent of fish consumed in the U.S. was imported from other countries.

The New England Fishermen’s Stewardship Association (NEFSA) reacted to Kennedy’s announcement, saying in a statement shared to the social platform X that the U.S.-made label is a “major win” for Americans.

“We believe U.S. seafood is the most sustainably harvested in the world, and this label gives consumers a simple, recognizable way to identify American-caught seafood while supporting our domestic fishing, processing, and retail industries,” NEFSA director of advocacy Jason Joyce said.

The new fishing initiative comes after the president’s trade war with Canada ruffled feathers with some in the industry.

The Maine Lobstermen’s Association said in August it feared becoming “collateral damage” in the trade war because Canada purchases large quantities of lobster from Maine fisheries.

data.title: About half concerned Republicans could try to overturn midterm results: Survey
data.description:
A new poll released Friday suggests half of Americans are concerned Republicans may try to overturn the results of November’s midterm election.

Fifty percent of respondents to the New York Times/Siena University survey said they were either “very” or “somewhat worried” the GOP may use “illegal means” to overturn the election, compared to 49 percent who are either “not too worried” or “not at all worried.”

A strong majority of Democrats — 86 percent — were among the share of likely voters who reported feeling worry about potential GOP election interference, and 52 percent independents felt the same. Even 10 percent of Republicans say they are worried their own party would overturn the results.

NYT/Siena also asked respondents if they feared Democrats may overturn the results, and 31 percent said they were — a group mainly consisting of Republicans.

Still, similar shares of Democratic, Republican and independents respondents to the NYT/Siena poll said they trusted midterm results would be accurate. And, across all parties, likely voters’ trust reached 74 percent.

President Trump has pushed claims of voter fraud for years, mainly when he or his party loses. Courts and election officials have consistently debunked or found no evidence for claims of widespread fraud in U.S. elections.

Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters Thursday the Justice Department (DOJ) has no intention “to improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process.” However, he did not rule out the potential for the DOJ to intervene in or block states from verifying election results.

On Friday morning, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.

The DOJ argued that, because another candidate with the same name is on the ballot, the election is not fair and could confuse voters. Sen. Sullivan is identified on the ballot with his Republican and incumbent status to differentiate himself from the other Dan Sullivan.

The poll was conducted Oct. 12-19 among 3,494 likely voters nationwide. The margin of error is 1.9 percentage points

data.title: Cook Political Report shifts Ohio governor's race from toss-up to lean Democrat
data.description:
The Cook Political Report is shifting a closely watched gubernatorial contest toward Democrats after a controversial campaign ad shook up the race.

The nonpartisan election forecaster moved the governor’s race in Ohio from “toss up” to “lean Democrat,” now favoring Amy Acton (D) to beat Vivek Ramaswamy (R) in the Buckeye State.

The race was the source of national attention after Ramaswamy debuted an ad with Acton’s estranged mother, who claims Acton is a “liar” and encourages voters not to elect her as Ohio governor.

Acton was removed from her mother’s custody at age 12. Her campaign said that she was sexually abused by her stepfather, who her mother remained with until his death.

The ad was widely condemned by Democrats and even some Republicans, including current Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R). Still, President Trump and Vice President Vance have both vehemently defended the ad.

Jessica Taylor, Cook Political Report’s Senate and governor’s editor, wrote in her analysis that Republicans they have talked to do not think the ad was a smart move.

“We haven’t talked to a GOP source who thought this was a good idea,” Taylor wrote. “This is not the kind of TV ad you run if you’re winning — or even if you’re confident you can. Recent polls were trending in Acton’s direction even before the bombshell ad became a national news story.”

Cook conducted a poll of the Ohio gubernatorial race before the ad was released and found Acton leading Ramaswamy by five points. Sabato’s Crystal Ball, another nonpartisan election forecaster, also changed its rating from “toss up” to “leans Democratic” earlier this week.

Acton’s fundraising has surged since the release of the ad, which Ramaswamy’s campaign is now spending $4 million to put on the air.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Acton a 62 percent chance of victory.

data.title: How will Democrats address UFO sightings if returned to the majority?
data.description:
Unidentified flying objects (UFOs) have long captivated Americans — a majority of whom, recent polling suggests, believe the government is hiding information about the phenomena. And the debate has also made its way to Capitol Hill.

In recent years, conversations surrounding UFOs, which the government now refers to as unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAPs), have heated up on both sides of the congressional political aisle.

In 2022, under a Democratic majority, a House Intelligence subcommittee held the first congressional hearing on UFOs in over five decades. Two officials leading the Pentagon’s UAP task force testified, with one making clear they were encouraging pilots to report sightings.

Americans still remain distrustful of the government’s handling of these phenomena. An August Gallup poll found that, while nearly half of Americans are skeptical that UFOs are of extraterrestrial origin, 78 percent believe the government knows more about the sightings than it tells the public.

In line with the public’s fascination, the second Trump administration has declassified files on UFOs and created a new governance board to coordinate investigations into reports of sightings.

Some lawmakers have taken an active role in calling for government transparency on the topic. And, with Democrats likely to take back control of the House next year, The Hill has broken down how the party’s UFO clarity advocates may address investigations and declassifications.

GOP keeps the reins of the UAP Caucus

Democratic leadership has previously backed efforts to increase transparency surrounding federal UFO investigations. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), Democrats’ likely House speaker choice should the party reclaim the lower chamber and current Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) step down, said in 2023 he supported sharing data on the phenomena with the public whenever feasible.

“I do support transparency to the extent this information that can be put into the public domain that is enlightening, one way or the other, and perhaps is able to dismiss some of the conspiracy theories that exist increasingly in our society,” Jeffries said in July 2023, as reported by The Hill’s broadcasting partner, NewsNation.

But Congress also has a caucus already dedicated to investigating and declassifying UFO information.

In 2023, Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) founded the UAP Caucus, which currently includes himself as well as Reps. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.), Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.), Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), Eric Burlison (R-Mo.) and Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.).

The caucus is “dedicated to the study, disclosure, and policy development surrounding” UFOs, according to its website, and hopes to expand the group to include the Senate.

Moskowitz is the caucus’s only Democrat, and he is in a tough battle for reelection after Florida Republicans redrew the state’s congressional districts. Two more members are set to leave the caucus, as Mace is retiring and Ogles lost renomination.

But the caucus also includes “honorable mentions” — members, including senators, who are not technically part of the caucus but are “instrumental” in supporting its goals.

‘Honorable mention’ Democrats support the cause

The Hill reached out to House Democrats running for reelection who are listed as either members or “honorable mentions” of the UAP Caucus.

Rep. Andre Carson (D-Ind.), one of the caucus’s honorable mentions, accused the Trump administration in a statement sent to The Hill of having “slow walked” UFO reporting and investigation transparency efforts. He specifically singled out a “historical UAP record report” and called for its immediate release.

“I’m calling for the immediate release of this report, which is expected to provide additional findings of historical military and intelligence investigations of UAP, including how incidents were investigated, the role of classified programs, and whether relevant activities were appropriately disclosed to Congress,” Carson said.

During the 2022 House hearing, Carson pushed to destigmatize UFO reporting for pilots and other military officials. The Indiana Democrat said at the time the stigma around the phenomena had “gotten in the way of good intelligence reporting,” as he alleged some pilots “were laughed at” when the reported unidentified aircraft.

Carson is a member of the House Intelligence Committee. Other House Democrats on the UAP Caucus “honorable mentions” list include Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.), Ro Khanna (Calif.) and Jamie Raskin (Md.).

Musk ups his midterm spending in final stretch

The tech mogul has spent more than $442 million in the midterm elections, after pouring another $76.8 million into his super PAC over the past month, campaign finance filings show.

© Susan Walsh, Associated Press

America PAC, which Musk launched during the 2024 elections, received the influx of cash from the SpaceX and Tesla CEO over the course of about a week in October, according to the super PAC’s last filing before the midterms.

 

This comes on top of the $366 million he had already spent so far on the upcoming elections.

 

He gave a combined $276 million to his super PAC and various Republican groups in the three-month stretch between July and September alone.

 

Musk has spent heavily backing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) amid a tight Senate race against Democrat James Talarico.

 

He gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC backing Republican Senate candidates, in two increments in September that were each disbursed to a Texas super PAC backing Paxton a day later.

 

Musk also gave $10 million to the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which is supporting Paxton, in addition to sending $20 million to a House GOP super PAC, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association.

data.title: West Virginia AG subpoenas environmental groups
data.description:
West Virginia’s attorney general has sent investigative subpoenas to environmental advocacy organizations – something the groups are describing as a retaliatory attack on their First Amendment rights.

West Virginia Rivers Coalition and 350.org filed a lawsuit this week saying that they and at least four other organizations received subpoenas from the office of West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey.

The demands seek information about the organizations’ public statements about climate change and energy, requests for donations, ties to renewable energy companies and more. 

They asked a federal court in West Virginia to halt enforcement of the subpoenas, saying they violate the organizations’ rights to free speech and calling them “baseless and retaliatory.”

Meanwhile, at least one other group, the Sierra Club, said they received a subpoena that was later withdrawn – after they informed the attorney general’s office of their intent to sue over it.

“While we are glad to see the West Virginia attorney general withdraw his sweeping subpoena after we informed him of our plans to file a federal lawsuit, his threats to silence and intimidate us and other groups remain,” said Loren Blackford, executive director of the Sierra Club. 

Blackford said the probe was unprecedented.

“We’ve seen nothing like this,” she said. 

The Hill has reached out to McCuskey’s office for comment.

In the past, congressional Republicans have subpoenaed and otherwise sought to investigate environmental groups. Earlier this year, Florida’s attorney general also subpoenaed environmental law-related organizations.

data.title: Secret Service closes road near White House due to suspicious package
data.description:
The U.S. Secret Service and D.C. police are investigating reports of a “suspicious item” near the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, which resulted in a road closure.

“Around 2:40 p.m., on October 23, 2026, Secret Service Police were notified of a suspicious item near 17th St. and Pennsylvania Avenue,” according to a statement from a Secret Service spokesperson to The Hill’s partner network NewsNation.

Out of an “abundance of caution,” the roads were closed in the area, the statement said.

The Metropolitan Police Department and other partners responded to the scene, according to the statement. It is an ongoing investigation.

The Embassy of Ireland, located in the same area, said it is “currently closed due to an ongoing security incident in the area, which has resulted in a number of street closures,” in a post on social platform X.

“Citizens in the area should heed the advice of local authorities,” the post said.

Earlier today in a similar incident, authorities investigated reports of a suspicious package near the Ukrainian Embassy. The embassy was evacuated before it reopened later as the item was deemed not harmful.

data.title: Paxton sues OpenAI, Altman for failing to warn Texans about ChatGPT's 'dangers'
data.description:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) sued OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman on Friday, accusing the company of failing to warn consumers about the potential dangers from its AI models.

The lawsuit alleges the ChatGPT maker is running afoul of a Texas consumer protection law and kids’ online safety law, underscoring warnings about the technology’s risks from AI leaders, including Altman.

“Despite these incredible dangers, Altman and OpenAI have not only barreled ahead in creating these risks but have done so by unlawfully deceiving Texans about the safety, accuracy, and reliability of their products,” the complaint reads.

“Defendants have built an artificial intelligence empire on the backs of Texans by deceiving them, while at the same time endangering public health,” it continues.

While their products are marketed as “trustworthy, reliable, and safe,” Paxton argues ChatGPT is prone to errors and hallucinations, in which AI tools produce fake results.

He suggests this “unreliability is dangerous,” pointing to users who have relied on incorrect or misleading healthcare information from ChatGPT.

The Texas attorney general also alleges OpenAI has failed to put in place proper safeguards for minors as required under the state’s Securing Children Online Through Parental Empowerment (SCOPE) Act.

Paxton further argues the company cannot control its technology, highlighting a series of recent incidents in which AI agents hacked into other organizations or acted in unexpected ways.

The Hill has reached out to OpenAI for comment.

Eight other states — Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Montana, Iowa, Kansas, West Virginia and Nebraska — sued the ChatGPT maker earlier this month, similarly arguing the company mislead users about the safety of its chatbot.

Florida separately sued OpenAI in June, alleging it promoted a product it knew could harm consumers.

“With the rapid advancement of AI technology, OpenAI has the responsibility to protect users and warn them of the many dangers of its platform,” Paxton said in a statement Friday. “I will fight to protect Texans from the harms of AI and ensure that powerful technology companies are not above the law.”

Paxton is currently facing off against Democrat James Talarico in a tight race for the Lone Star state’s Senate seat.

Despite President Trump’s forceful embrace of AI, Paxton and several other GOP candidates have sought some distance on issues surrounding the technology, most notably data centers.

The Texas attorney general unveiled a plan in August to place restrictions on the controversial AI infrastructure if he is elected to the Senate.
